The Mandala
the palace of Sarvavid Vairocana

Sktmaṇḍala Tibdkyil 'khor DeitySarvavid Vairocana · kun rig TantraSarvadurgatipariśodhana

A mandala is the plan of a palace drawn from above, with its walls and its inhabitants laid flat on the ground. This page takes one painting, a seventeenth-century Tibetan mandala of the All-Knowing Vairocana, and stands it back up into the palace it depicts, built from the painting's own pixels and nothing else. Every element can be clicked and read.

Chapter I

The painting

A mandala (Sanskrit maṇḍala, “circle”; Tibetan dkyil 'khor, “centre and surround”) is the residence of a deity and its retinue, set out around a centre. In the tantric practice of Tibet it is painted on cloth, laid out in coloured sand, built in three dimensions, or imagined in meditation. In every form it is a palace with the deities in their places, and the painted version is its ground plan.

This painting shows the mandala of Sarvavid Vairocana, the principal mandala of the Tantra Purifying Bad Rebirths (Sarvadurgatipariśodhana). The tantra belongs to the Yoga class, the third of the four classes into which Tibetan tradition sorts the tantras. It was composed in India in the early eighth century and translated into Tibetan soon afterwards. It teaches twelve mandalas whose rites purify the causes of rebirth in the three lower destinies, as a being in hell, a hungry ghost or an animal, and in Tibet it became the tantra of funerals.

The painting was made in Tibet in the seventeenth century, in ground mineral pigment on cotton. Around the mandala sit the teachers through whom the practice was handed down: above, on clouds, the Buddha, Vajrapāṇi and the early Indian and Tibetan masters; below, twelve Tibetan lamas and four protectors. Their inscriptions run from Rinchen Zangpo through the founders of the Sakya school to Ngorchen Kunga Zangpo and two figures of the late sixteenth century: a lineage that runs through the Ngor branch of the Sakya school.

The mandala itself is a set of nested enclosures. From the outside in: a ring of gold, a ring of vajras, a ring of 128 worldly deities, a green courtyard, the outer palace with sixty figures, the inner palace, a lotus of sixteen petals, and a circle holding the five buddhas and four goddesses. The thirty-seven deities of the inner palace are the mandala proper; everything outside them surrounds and protects them.

The model at the top of the page is built from the photograph of the painting. Press Raise the palace and the painting stands up into the building it records; press Walk in to go through it from the rim to the centre with a note on each element.

Chapter II

Reading a plan

A mandala painting is a plan: the palace seen from directly above. A plan shows the ground and nothing that rises from it, so the painter adds the elevations by laying them down flat. A wall is drawn as a strip lying outward from the line it stands on, with its foot along that line and its top along the outer edge. A figure is drawn lying on its back, its seat toward the centre and its head toward the rim. A portico over a door is drawn as coloured tiers stacked outward from the door, and the ornaments on a roof are drawn beyond the wall that carries them.

The orientation follows the entrance. The main gate faces east and lies at the bottom of the painting, so that the viewer stands where the disciple stands on entering; west is at the top, south on the left, north on the right. Each quarter takes the colour of its direction.

east · blue · bottom south · yellow · left west · red · top north · green · right centre · white

The model applies the rule in reverse. Each wall rises from the inner edge of its painted bands; its faces show the bands in order from foot to top, and its top shows the plan. Each figure is cut out along its painted outline, halo and flames included, and stands up on the line of its seat. Each ornament painted beyond a wall moves onto that wall. Seen straight down, the tops of the walls are exactly the painted bands; the Plan view lays the whole model flat again, and then it is the painting.

What the model adds and what it leaves out
  • Heights. The painting gives a plan and no elevations. The heights of walls, gatehouses and pedestals are the model's; the courses of each wall keep the proportions of the painted bands, stretched upward.
  • Roofs. The texts describe a roofed palace. The model leaves it open, as the painting does, so that the inside can be seen.
  • Figures. The deities are imagined in the round, seated on lotus and moon seats. The model stands the painted images up as flat panels. Each panel carries the painting on both faces, so from behind a figure is seen in reverse, as through glass. Vairocana has four faces; the painter shows the three that can be seen from the front, and the model keeps that view.
  • The ground. Once the palace is raised, every zone of the floor takes one flat colour, the commonest colour of its painted ground: the four quarters of each palace floor, the nine compartments of the central circle, the lotus, the courtyard, the sky above the mandala and the earth below it. The small ornaments, clouds and scrolls painted on the ground are left out. The brocade border stays as painted.
  • The centre. The painter seats Vairocana in the middle of the central square. A figure standing up on the line of its seat would stand at the square's eastern edge, so the model moves him to the centre.
  • The gateways. The wheel, deer and parasol over each outer gate are raised together, cut along their painted outlines; the arch around them keeps its measured shape.
  • The surroundings. The lineage above and the protectors below are outside the palace; the model stands them up where they are painted, facing the viewer.

The inner palace holds 37 deities, the outer palace 60 figures, the ring 128: 225 figures inside the gold, and the painter's eight adepts besides. Outside the gold the painting has seventeen teachers above and sixteen figures below.

Chapter IV

The thirty-seven

The Tibetan name of the mandala gives its number: kun rig rnam par snang mdzad lha so bdun gyi dkyil 'khor, the thirty-seven-deity mandala of All-Knowing Vairocana. The same count, and most of the same figures, make up the Vajradhātu mandala, the central mandala of the Yoga tantras. The Tantra Purifying Bad Rebirths gives the four buddhas names of its own and puts the goddesses Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī and Tārā in the corners of the circle.

The painting labels none of the thirty-seven. The tantra places the groups; where it does not place the members of a group, the order below is the usual one.

PlaceDeityWhat it stands for
Chapter V

The five families

The five buddhas of the circle are the heads of five families (kula) into which the Yoga tantras sort everything in the mandala. Each family has a direction, a colour, an emblem, a wisdom, and an affliction of which that wisdom is the purified form. The tantra alludes to the emblems when it asks for the mandala to be marked with “vajras, jewels, lotuses, and crossed vajras”.

In this painting the ground of each quarter takes the family colour, while the four buddhas have colours of their own set by the tantra: the buddha of the east is pale pink on a blue ground, the buddha of the south dark blue on a yellow ground.

QuarterHereElsewhereFamily · emblemWisdomAffliction

Tibetan exposition extends the scheme to the five aggregates that make up a person and to the elements, and here the systems part company: the aggregate and the element given to each family differ from one tantra to another. The first three columns come from the painting and the tantra; the last three follow the common Tibetan presentation of the five wisdoms.

Chapter VI

The palace as the path

The tantra prescribes the palace: square, four gates with porticos, a staircase of four steps, lions and elephants, garlands, bells and yak-tail whisks. The meaning of these things is left to the commentators. Tibetan commentary reads the architecture as an inventory of the qualities of awakening, so that entering the palace is a picture of travelling the path.

One reading, from the fourteenth-century Nyingma master Longchenpa in The Great Chariot, is given below. Other commentators, and the commentaries on other tantras, give other lists; they agree in treating every part of the building as a part of the path.

Part of the palaceQuality of the path
The four gatesthe four immeasurables: love, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity
The four porticosthe four foundations of mindfulness: body, feeling, mind, phenomena
The wall of five layersthe five wisdoms
The eight pillarsthe eightfold noble path
Bells, garlands of suns and moons, yak tails, jewelsthe five faculties and the five powers
Garlands and pendantsthe seven factors of awakening
The eavesgreat compassion
The cornicesthe unchanging nature of mind
The parasolsthe sphere of reality
The wheelsthe four noble truths

Longchenpa writes about the palaces of other tantras, and this mandala has no painted pillars or cornices. The list shows the kind of reading the tradition gives to a mandala palace in general; the Tantra Purifying Bad Rebirths offers no gloss of its own.

Chapter VII

What the mandala is for

The story

The tantra opens in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. A god named Vimalamaṇiprabha has died, and Śakra, king of the gods, asks the Buddha where he has been reborn. In the great Avīci hell, the Buddha answers, where he will suffer for twelve thousand years before passing through lesser hells, the births of an animal and a hungry ghost, and a long human life of misery. Śakra begs for a way to free him, and the Buddha teaches the mantras and the mandala of Sarvavid. The rites are performed on the god's behalf and he is restored to heaven.

The Buddha then gives the cause. In an earlier life the god had been a prince who killed his father and caused his mother's death, and who later repented before a sage and died of grief. The repentance won him birth as a god; the earlier deeds were delayed, not removed. The prince was Vimalamaṇiprabha, the father was Śakra, and the sage was Śākyamuni himself. The story establishes that the rites may be performed by others, on behalf of someone already dead.

Entering the mandala

At initiation the disciple is led into the mandala blindfolded with silk, holding a vajra and a lotus, and throws a flower onto it. The family of the deity on which the flower falls is the disciple's own, and the tantra promises accomplishment through that deity. The disciple then takes the vows, with an oath sealed by water:

“This is the water of hell for you. If you transgress your vow, it will scorch you.”The Tantra Purifying Bad Rebirths 1.79, tr. Kris L. Anderson

The disciple enters from the east. In the model, the east gate is at the front, where the viewer stands.

For the dead

The tantra says that the bodies of the dead, placed in the mandala and consecrated, are freed even from hell and reborn among the gods. The rites of Sarvavid, called Kunrig in Tibetan, became a regular part of Tibetan funerals, and Himalayan Art Resources notes their use in the consecration of new temples as well. Newar Buddhists in the Kathmandu Valley use the Sanskrit version of the tantra in their funerary rites to the present day.

In Tibetan history

The tantra was one of the few that the Tibetan empire approved for translation and circulation in the ninth century. The Chronicle of Ba records Sarvavid Vairocana among the central deities of the main temple at Samyé, Tibet's first monastery, founded in 779. The same chronicle tells of a debate at the funeral of King Tri Songdetsen (d. c. 800) over whether his funeral should follow Buddhist rites or the older ones, won by the Buddhists, who declared that royal funerals would follow this tantra from then on; that account may be considerably later than the rest of the chronicle. Rinchen Zangpo performed the funeral of King Lha Lama Yeshé Ö by its methods in the eleventh century.

Chapter VIII

Around the mandala

Thirty-nine figures carry inscriptions, numbered here as in Laura A. Weinstein's key for Himalayan Art Resources. Many are worn away; where the key identifies a figure from a fragment or from its place, the identification is given as the key gives it. Two figures have no number: Śākyamuni at the top centre and Śrī Devī among the protectors, named on the front of the painting as lha mo.

About this page

A study supplement to The River of Dharma. The painting is identified, and its inscribed figures read, after Himalayan Art Resources, item 773: Jeff Watt's description and Laura A. Weinstein's inscription key. The description of the mandala follows the Tantra Purifying Bad Rebirths (Toh 483), chapter 1, in the translation of Kris L. Anderson for 84000 (2026); quotations are from that translation. The history of the tantra in Tibet follows the introduction to the same translation.

On names. The painting labels the lineage and the protectors but none of the deities of the mandala. Where the tantra names a group without placing its members (the sixteen vajra beings, the eight offering goddesses, the four goddesses of the circle), the positions given here follow the usual arrangement of the Yoga-tantra mandala and are marked as such in the text. The sixteen bodhisattvas are the usual set beginning with Maitreya; the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, wrathful guardians and the 128 worldly deities are described as groups.

On the model. Every surface takes its colour from the photograph of the painting. The plan was measured at full resolution (1981 × 2500 pixels): the circles by fitting to the painted edges, the walls and gates by hand. The figures are cut along their painted outlines: the niches of the palace by fitting each arch to the painted edge, the teachers of the lineage from outlines traced by hand and refined by colour (GrabCut), the four protectors along the tongues of their flames; each halo is a circle fitted to its painted edge. Every outline was checked against the painting. The photograph has 1981 × 2500 pixels; the camera stops where one pixel of it covers one pixel of the screen. The heights of walls and gates are the model's own, as are the pedestals under the five buddhas. Chapter II lists the other differences.

On the symbolism. The tantra prescribes the forms of the mandala and explains few of them. The correspondences given in chapters V and VI come from later Tibetan exposition, which differs from one text and one school to another; the tables give one common set and say whose it is.
